utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, with the case manager, Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could the Defence introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic's Defence, Edina Residovic, Stephane Bourgon, and Mirna Milanovic as legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Mr. Rodney Dixon, Mr. Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We wish to bid good afternoon to all those present, so good afternoon to the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence, as well as the accused. We have a witness planned for today, and I think some protective measures will be requested. For that purpose, I would like to ask the registrar that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you just told us that the younger ones went to the barracks there. Were you in fact also taken to the former JNA barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon your arrival there, did anyone welcome you or make any kind of announcement to the group of people arriving by lorry at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know there were some troops and officers. Fikret Cuskic was there. And they said -- when we arrived there, they said, "Welcome." They said, "You'll be with us now." It was all right at the beginning, and then they said later, "You will have to report. You'll have to be mobilised," and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what position Fikret Cuskic held at the time you arrived at the former JNA barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was a battalion or brigade commander, something like that. I know that he was a high-ranking officer. He was some sort of a commander, either of a battalion or of a brigade. I think he was the commander of a battalion there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which battalion or brigade he commanded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 17th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reaction upon being notified that you were being mobilised into the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first asked whether it would be possible for me to rest, first of all, to come to my senses. They knew very well what it was like -- what it had been like in the town in which I had come from. They knew the living conditions and the threats we had faced. And then there were some others who asked me, "What are you saying? You want to join the Chetniks. You don't want to join the Muslims," and so on. And then I started quarreling, resisting, and the tension rose. And finally, I know -- I remember that they took me down into a basement. I was wearing black trousers and a black jacket. And they said, "Look at the Ustasha. He's dressed like a Ustasha," and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the basement of the building that you were taken down into. What was in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a big hall, a long hall. You go down a flight of stairs, and then to the left at the end I could see -- this is something I saw later. I didn't realise this immediately. I was scared when I saw the basement. I didn't look around a lot, but they took me to the right part and locked me up in a room. It was a small narrow room. In fact, it wasn't small. There were a number of people who were lying down there and sitting in the room. I entered the room, and they left me among those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us approximately how many people were in that room and the ethnicity of those people, if you know it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There may have been about ten of them. There were Muslims, and I don't know how many -- I know of about two Croats who were there at the time, because when I got in, I didn't communicate with them much. It's not really a place where you would engage in any conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then this one, who had brought me there, who had shoved me into the basement, I had about 500 German marks on me, which he took from me. And later on this military policeman - because he was a military policeman - I would see him, later on in Zenica. He was Alagic's bodyguard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us he was a military policeman. How did you know he was a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They all wear those white police markings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of clothing was this individual wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall where on the uniform the white police markings were worn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On their sleeves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, were there any insignia? Or did you otherwise know what military unit this military policeman belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It said the "17th Krajina" and the "27th Krajina Brigade in formation." But the 17th Krajina Brigade was the only unit there, no other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "it was the only unit there," do you mean the building that you were detained in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that entire barracks. They were there and another building of the 27th Brigade. That was the brigade in the process of formation. They were in another building. But as far as I know, it was never formed. That brigade was supposed to be the 27th Banja Luka Brigade. However, after everything that happened there, that brigade was never formed, and all those people from Banja Luka fled from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please describe for the Trial Chamber the room in the basement that you were kept in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a room of about 6 or 7 metres long and about 3 or 4 metres wide, perhaps. To one side, there were wooden planks on which we lay down. And this was below street level, so that the window, which was high up next to the ceiling -- and if anyone wanted to look inside, he would have to kneel down to peep inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe if the room you were in had any kind of door.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know there were iron bars. I'm not sure. I think there was a door, but it was very hot and there was no air, so the door was quite frequently left open and only the bars remained. So there was a door and iron bars, and this door led to a small corridor, and then there were large iron bars, which led to the right, to the rooms where they did the beatings and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection as to how many rooms were located in the basement of the building where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really tell, but behind those bars, the first set of bars, then I think there were another one or two rooms behind those bars. I'm not quite sure. I couldn't walk around much. But there was at least another one room, but not more than two or three, behind those bars that I mentioned. That part of the corridor was walled -- partitioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned "that part of the corridor," Witness. Were there other parts of the corridor? And if so, were there additional rooms or offices on the other parts of the corridor in the basement of that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were other rooms. There were other rooms in another part of the corridor. And at the very other end was a military prison that -- they called it that -- and that is where they held prisoners in detention who had committed certain errors, members of the 17th Krajina Brigade. They were their soldiers, but they were being disciplined. They had committed certain errors or violated rules, and they were being held there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know to what purpose any of the other rooms in the basement of that building were being put to use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In one of those rooms, they beat us. And later on, when - I don't know how to put it - when the civilian police got me out of there with the help of people from my town, I later saw that they used it as their command. The operations group -- the commander of the operations group would be sitting there when fighting against the Croats. Cuskic was there and all the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which operations group had offices in the basement of that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During those battles, there was also a clinic, where they brought the wounded combatants for treatment, in that same corridor, in one or two of those rooms. When you walk down the steps, close to the staircase there was this clinic for wounded soldiers. Then to the left was the command and the communications room. And these high-ranking officers, who were in command of the fighting, they sat there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I want to return now to the time when you first arrived in this basement cell. Do you recall approximately what time it was when you were first taken to this cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was late afternoon, something like that. It was in the afternoon. I can't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us there were about ten people in the room when you arrived. Did you know any of these people or had you ever seen any of these people before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of these people did you know, and from where did you know them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew one of them, one or two. I knew them from before. We were from the same town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had these people arrived with you on the lorries from your home town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were already there when I arrived. They had been there from before. They may have come earlier on, but not on that day, not on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- upon your arrival or shortly thereafter, did you discuss with the other ten people in the basement cell why they were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why the other ten people were being detained in the basement of the former JNA barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all accused of being either Chetniks or Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell -- or were there any visible signs of injury on any of the other ten people at the time when you first arrived in that room in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I think the witness said yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber what types of visible injuries you noticed on your fellow detainees at the time of your arrival.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They all had -- they were all black and blue. They had all been beaten up, each and every one of them, and they had bruises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened to you in the evening or night of your first day in the basement of the former JNA barracks in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When night fell, they took me outside and they beat me for several hours, forcing me to admit that I had been with the Chetniks, that I had been in Kozarac, in Prijedor, and I don't know where else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you say "they took me outside," can you tell the Trial Chamber who it was that took you outside.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ferguson and this other one, who was the commander of the camp, as they called him. Ferguson was the name of the person who beat everyone. I would just like to say that the entire 17th Krajina Brigade knew about him, the command, and even the command threatened ordinary soldiers, "If you don't listen, Ferguson will get hold of you." So this is not the first time for them to hear of him. This Ferguson was a big Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. guy, enormous. I heard from -- I heard he came from a village near Jajce, Donji Vakuf or something like that. And he would beat everyone inside. Later on I saw that even the commander of the prison - and it was a prison of the 17th Krajina Brigade - even he was afraid of him. And once he drew a pistol on him, threatening to kill him -- rather, Ferguson did. He threatened to kill him. Because he is so big, that is why they nicknamed him Ferguson, after a tractor known as Ferguson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me -- let me stop you there, Witness. So Ferguson was a nickname for this person who took you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what his real name was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They all knew him as Ferguson. The whole of Travnik knew him only as Ferguson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, now, you told us that Ferguson and the person who was known as the commander of the camp took you outside. Did they actually take you outside of the building, or did they take you outside of the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside those iron bars, the first set of bars and then the second set of bars, so there in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the corridor in the basement of the building, the JNA barracks in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this person Ferguson and the person that you've called the commander of the camp, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if they also had the white military police armbands on their uniforms, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty. I think the person who was the commander did have an armband. I think that Ferguson did too, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that you were beaten. How long did this beating last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two, three, four hours. I don't know. I can't say. Time either flies or stretches out endlessly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than Ferguson and the commander of the camp, did any other soldiers or military policemen participate in this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Anyone could come in, any one of the members of that 17th Battalion. Anyone could come in and beat. But so did the military police of the 17th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many people participated in the beating you received on the first day you were detained in the former JNA barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three of them together, then two or three would be sitting down, taking a rest. And then when one group tires, then the next group takes over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you beaten by this group of soldiers and military policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With a spade handle or a pickaxe handle. I'm not quite sure. There was a pickaxe and iron bars and the police truncheons, and they kicked us a lot. They had boots on their feet, and they would kick us with them. Then they would take a big towel, and one end they held in their hand and the other they soaked in water. Then they would beat with that wet towel wherever they could, but mostly on our backs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were being beaten, Witness, did any of these individuals who were beating you say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They say, "Confess. Why were you with the Chetniks?" And I said, "I wasn't with the Chetniks. I was mobilised. I was at the beginning only in Croatia for a month. And when I saw that the Chetniks had arrived singing Chetnik songs," and I explained to them that an Ilija was killed from behind, that the Yugoslav army had killed him, had shot him in the back, and he was with us. And when I saw this, the first chance I had I grabbed to escape from that battlefield to reach my own town. And later I had problems there. I said I wasn't a Chetnik. "Then you're an Ustasha," they said. "Why are you wearing black?" They were just finding excuses to beat me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what happened after the beating finished several hours later? What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then in a way they helped me reach the room. And once I was thrown inside, I don't really remember. I don't really know what happened after that. I don't know. Somebody may have helped me. Someone may have given me some water. I know when people were brought back from beatings they asked for water. Maybe I asked for water too, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how long were you detained in the basement of the former JNA barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seven or eight days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the remaining seven or eight days that you were detained there, were you physically mistreated on any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've just told us about being beaten on the first night you were detained. You remained in the basement of the former JNA barracks in Travnik for another six or seven days. On any other day were you similarly mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Every night they beat me, every night, as they did the others who were detained with me. And they would take other detainees who were there, and they beat me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe these other beatings for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all the same. The beating was the same. People would come in; other soldiers take their place and start beating; then the military policemen, the brigade police of the 17th Brigade. One group beat me. Then others beat me. The detainees beat me. Every night it was the same story all over again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it, Witness, that the detainees beat you, your fellow detainees? Why did they beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were forced to do. When they were too tired to beat, then they would bring others, other detainees, and say to them, "You beat him." And if they refused, then they'd say, "Beat him or I will beat you," and then they do. We'd known each other for a long time, and yet he had to beat me. It was hard for him. And afterwards, when we went back to the room, he would come and complain and apologise, "I'm sorry, but I had to do it." And I'd say, "Never mind. I forgive you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you say "we'd known each other for a long time," are you referring to one of the other detainees that you'd known from your home town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am referring to him, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, of the approximate ten people who were detained with you in the JNA -- former JNA barracks in Travnik, did all of those people survive the detention in that basement cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. One man died one night. And he was taken out in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you recall about that incident, who this person was, the circumstances of his death.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have any contact with him. I know he was a Croat and he was young. That night I think he was the first they took out to beat. And when they shoved him back in, they took me out. And when I returned, they were saying, "He's dying. He's done for." No one can help each other. We couldn't help each other, because if they saw us helping each other, they would start beating again. Someone beat on the door, calling, "Ferguson," and then he came and said, "So what? Let him die." And then he said, "Well, he'll die here. Take him away." And then he said, "Nothing's wrong with him," and later on they took him out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he was still alive when they took him out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. Perhaps this is the approximate time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, Mr. Mundis, will you put your question to the witness once again, because we didn't hear the answer. Will you repeat your question to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when they took this young Croat out of the cell, was he still alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took him out of the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers, Ferguson and the Krajina soldiers. Someone was with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We're going to have our technical break. It is quarter to 4.00. We will have a 25-minute break and resume at ten past 4.00. So will the registrar take all the necessary measures for the witness not to be seen by the public gallery. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume, and we'll go into open session. The Prosecution may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask that the witness be shown the electronic version of Prosecution Exhibit 39, which was tendered into evidence last week. I'd like to show him the electronic version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the screen in front of you should have Prosecution Exhibit 39. Do you see that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see a building. I see a building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this building is that you see before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's the building in Travnik, the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that another photograph be shown to the witness, with the assistance of the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could please take a look at the photograph on the machine to your right. I know it's also visible on the screen in front of you, but if you could please look to the photograph to your right. Do you recognise what's depicted in the photograph that you see in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's the basement we were in, that there are other photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could please date that photograph and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you prefer the pseudonym or --...? It needs to be taken off the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness XE, write down on the photograph your first and last names, make a note of today's date, the 26th of January, 2004, and write "XE" on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is the Prosecution tendering this -- requesting that this be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Mr. President. We'd ask that that be tendered under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll show this photograph to the Defence and to the accused; to the Prosecution -- they haven't seen it yet. They haven't seen what has been noted. Show it to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Mr. Registrar, could we have an (redacted) number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The (redacted) number will be P49, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: (redacted). And this had been agreed with the Serbian army, because when I got there, on the first day in Travnik he saw me. We spoke to each other briefly, and then he heard a story about the military police over there, that they'd been beating someone. And they said, "We'll beat him, but he just won't collapse." They said, "We'll beat him every night." I got used to those beatings. The Serbs would beat me. But when I'm beaten by Serbs, it's not so bad as when the Muslims beat me. The Serbs find fault with me because I'm a Muslim. And then when I think I'm safe, when I'm with Muslims, then I'm beaten by Muslims. Why does this happen? I don't know. I thought I'd solved this, but then that lawyer who had helped a lot of people, he came to the conclusion that I was that person. He put two and two together. And then he went to the civilian police and the civilian police came and they contacted -- they phoned the police in the 3rd Corps -- the military police in the 3rd Corps, and together with the civilian police they arrived, and there was a lot of confusion then because after those beatings, those daily beatings, I was no longer able to stand up. I could only remain lying down. They weren't able to get me out. The police of the 17th Krajina Brigade didn't allow them to take me out. The Krajina Corps military police and the civilian police and that lawyer, they were there. And some special police forces came. They wanted to take me out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me briefly interrupt. Do you know who the high-ranking officer who came and ordered them to release you was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a fairly high-ranking officer in the military police of the 3rd Corps. That was the corps police who got me out. Whereas, those who were detaining me, they were members of the police of the 17th Krajina Brigade. And those who took me out were the police from the corps and the civilian police and the commanders who had appeared down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw that they had -- that he was very respected. They respected him. They weren't afraid of him, but, you know, the kind of respect they show for high-ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once this high-ranking officer military police officer arrived, were you in fact then taken away from the basement cell in the barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't able to walk. They took me out on a stretcher. An ambulance came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the civilian police station in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do upon arrival at the civilian police station in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was questioned by the civilian police. They made a record of the interrogation. They asked me some questions. They saw I had been beaten. They knew who had beaten me. They knew everything. But they asked me, "Who beat you?" I was sick. I'd been beaten. I said, "Leave me alone. You know who beat me. You know that very well." But they said, "You've got to make a statement, though." So they questioned me there, and I spent two or three hours there. Then someone called Esad came. And I think he was a security officer in the 17th Krajina Brigade. And they wanted to transfer me to the hospital from there. They wanted to transfer me from the police station to the hospital so that I could be provided with medical treatment. I was lucky in that I had withstood the beating better than others, perhaps. I don't know. But I managed to survive all those beatings, and they wanted to take me to hospital. But when he appeared, when this person called Esad, this security officer from the 17th Krajina Brigade, he said, "What do you mean a hospital? Taking him to a hospital would amount to a scandal, because the military police has been beating Muslims and so on." So he said, "Don't do it." Then a quarrel broke out. The civilian police and the corps military police wanted to transfer me to hospital, whereas the others didn't want to do so. I said, "Just take me somewhere so I can be provided with treatment. I'm going to die." (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that's what happened. And then somehow they agreed that they should avoid a scandal, that this shouldn't be made public knowledge, and they transferred me then. They agreed that I should go to the clinic and that I should be treated there. I -- then someone said something about someone having taken money. They said, "We'll find him. The corps police is here." And they found that military policeman, but they only found 300 German marks on him. He had already spent 200 marks, he said. So they returned 300 German marks to me and then they took me to that clinic. And I remained lying in that clinic and they fed me for a few days, turned me over to prevent me from getting bed sores. I wasn't able to turn over myself. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). He confiscated the photographs from him, so that the civilian police didn't have any photographs. Later all the medical documents disappeared, all the documents about being treated in the clinic. All of that disappeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you told the Trial Chamber that the civilian police said it would be reported to the corps, do you know what corps they were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the 3rd Corps. It was the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll redact page 37, line 3. We'll redact this from the transcript. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, approximately how long did you remain in the infirmary at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Over 20 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other people in the barracks infirmary at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were other people there. I was in a room. I think there were two or three beds in it, but I can't remember. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the other people who were in the infirmary at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date or month and year that you were discharged from the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. I was released. I was discharged -- well, I remember I was standing in front of the infirmary, in front of the entrance. The entrance was facing the village of Bojna. That was a Croatian village. And we were standing there. At the time, I was feeling better. I could walk. We were standing there, and the soldier Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who had set off to have a check-up in the infirmary fell down. We headed in that direction, and then we noticed that he'd been hit by a sniper. And I remember that that was the first person to be hit. I couldn't say whether he was killed or only wounded, but that was the first person to be hit on that day. (redacted). That's when the war with the Croats started for real. And then we moved into the basement. The infirmary moved into the basement, the same basement that I was previously detained in -- not the same basement, the same hall. It was in another room. The cell I was in was at one end of the hall, and at the other end of the hall. When we got down there, the command had already moved down there in the communications room and the infirmary had been moved there. They set up an infirmary down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I remained there. That was emptied at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, upon being discharged from the infirmary, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was fighting at the time, and I went around in the ambulance. I remember I -- I helped. We would collect the wounded with the ambulance. A civilian had been hit on the street. They said he had been hit. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) And while we were transferring him, he died. And I helped by going around in the ambulance, by driving around in the ambulance while the fighting was ongoing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, upon your discharge from the infirmary, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of the fighting -- the fighting didn't last for very long, not for a very long time. I was feeling better, and then they said I couldn't remain inside and that I had to leave. A lot of Croatian houses had been abandoned. A lot of flats had been abandoned. Maybe not all of them, but a lot of Croats had left Travnik. So for a certain period of time I slept in the secondary school with the other refugees. And as I didn't have the status of a refugee, I tried to get the food I could. I'd buy food with my own money. And then I would sleep in those abandoned Croatian houses in the village there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "in the village there," was that still in the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bojna. I think that's the name, opposite the barracks. From that village, that's where the Croats attacked the barracks from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain in or around the town of Travnik following your release from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Several days. And when they said that the roads had been opened, someone told me, "You know, I think you should flee from here. A lot of noise has been made because of what happened to you. I believe that if you stay on" -- this is what he heard -- they heard that people from the Krajina Brigade would kill me. And then when I had the first opportunity of getting a lorry -- getting onto a lorry, I did that and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go in this lorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to a place, to a reception centre for refugees. That's where I slept on the floor for several days, like all the other refugees. And then when I arrived there, as I was -- as I had already been registered by the International Red Cross, I went there and asked the International Red Cross to help me flee from Bosnia, to help me be transferred, to give me either money or food or something like that. But they weren't able to do so. I had some German marks and I'd get a little food. Later I received some sort of a voucher which enabled me to get some bread and some tinned food. And then I looked for work. They said, "Go to the hospital." I'd go to the hospital --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what kind of police were in the Music School?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the police that was part of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date or month and year that you went to the Zenica Music School and spoke to the 7th Muslim Brigade police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was perhaps in June, but I don't really remember. In June, the end of June, the beginning of July. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke to the military police in the Zenica Music School, were you asked any questions? And if so, please tell the Trial Chamber what you were asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted). I'm afraid that they might kill me." And this policeman who was at the desk at the entrance to the building, he said, "Don't be afraid. They're drunks, trash." He said, "If they take you in here, they won't be able to touch you. We'll protect you." So he then asked me to examine something. I can't remember what I examined. It had to do with something from the Koran. He asked me to recite something. When I was small - when I was young - we'd go to the mosque. Children would go and I'd go too. I had learnt quite a lot from the Koran. He wanted to check whether I was a real Muslim or whether I was only pretending to be a Muslim. He said, "Very well. Go and report to the barracks in Bilmiste." I went there. I don't know if he gave me some sort of a document, piece of paper, but I went there and reported to them. They asked me what I knew to do. I said I knew how to work in the hospital. I knew how to drive. I can help with the work that is done in hospitals and with the wounded and so on. They asked me whether I was afraid of going to the field -- going into the field. I said no. They said, "Okay, go and see Hasan." Hasan saw me. He said, "You'll go with the company. Very well." So when I didn't go to the company, when the company wasn't in the field, I'd help in the infirmary. I'd help with the wounded, by putting bandages on them and so on. There were a lot of Hasans there. There was Hasan a technician, there was Hasan a doctor, there was another Hasan who was a doctor. There were a lot of them, and they were all called Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd ask that we briefly go into closed session so I can ask the witness a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going into private session now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. I went there at the beginning to get some supplies from someone over there. I wasn't driving. Another person was driving. He knew the route and everything. They said that there were some bandages there for the brigade, for the infirmary, bandages and other medical supplies for the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to Mehurici to retrieve these medical supplies, did you speak to any specific individuals or were you told to liaise with anyone in particular, or what were you told to do in order to obtain these medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. We went there. When we got there, we saw that there were many foreigners there. We went there. And I don't remember everything. And we collected those things. We picked them up. I don't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were these foreigners doing in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. They were there. They were living there. They were fighters, warriors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if these fighters and warriors were members of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told me when I went there. They told me, "They are our fighters over there. They belong to us." They told me that we were going to see them. Some of them wore insignia; some didn't. They didn't all wear insignia. Some wore the green insignia of the 7th Muslim; others didn't. Some had insignia; some didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness, the names or other designators of any of those subunits of the 7th Muslim Brigade that were in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were known as El Mujahed, El Mujahed. I was quite new there, and I was told that this was the El Mujahed Platoon and that we were going to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we please go into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber what happened once your unit arrived in Vares.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went with another company. I was assigned to another company. I said, "I'll go down there with you. I'll go into the attack with you." They said, "All right." On the way down there, they said Vares had been abandoned, the Croats have abandoned Vares. That was a report. They said that the night before they had broken through. They said, "I heard that the Blue Falcons have broken through and another sabotage brigade, but not part of the 7th Muslim Brigade. It was another brigade. They weren't part of the 7th Muslim Brigade." They said that the road was open and that the Croats had fled. We descended there. No one fired a shot. There were a few shells that came in our direction from somewhere. No one was wounded. We entered Vares. At the entrance to Vares, as soon as we entered, we entered Donji Vares and we saw in the window of a flat -- I don't know who it was, but a member of the Blue Falcons. He waved to us. A short time passed. And we came across a large group in some sort of a house. They were Croats and then some Muslims opened the windows and they said, "We are Muslims." They all gathered. And troops and UNPROFOR arrived. I think that they were Swedes. Yes, that's when the troops Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. dispersed. Everyone dispersed. No one looked at anyone any more, and then -- I don't know how to put it. Some sort of looting started. I don't know what to call it. People went from house to house, flat to flat. I no longer knew anyone. I lost track of everyone. I no longer remember how I got to Gornji Vares. In Gornji Vares it was chaos. Later I heard after the war these people have entered and those people entered, no one entered. It was the 7th Muslim Brigade that entered Vares and occupied it. And then towards nightfall the Sarajevo Swallows and men from Tuzla arrived. We were already there, and everyone took care of themselves. We were hungry, thirsty. And I remember that afterwards I found a beer somewhere. I thought I should open it up. And I was afraid because someone might report me to the police. We weren't allowed to drink, to do anything. I opened the beer and had a beer after so many years. I came across people driving cars, motorbikes, lorries, et cetera. And later other troops arrived, other troops from other corps. These troops came from all over the place. I remember that I met a civilian carrying a rifle. I asked him, "What's happening?" He said, "You are looting my town." He said, "I used to be a policeman here before the war. I'm a Muslim. What are you doing?" I said, "Leave me alone. See what the others are doing." It was chaos, complete chaos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've described people driving cars, motorbike, lorries, et cetera. Who were these people driving these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Troops, the troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any other type of personal property being looted, other than these various vehicles that you've described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't look into other people's vehicles. I didn't know what people had in their cars. But they said that there would be a checkpoint, that the brigade would set up a checkpoint at the exit from Vares, and they said that no appliance should be taken out, that the military police would confiscate everything. That's what we were told. Later on I left. I got out. I no longer remember how I managed to do so. I think we got out on foot. I remember some sort of camera when we were leaving. We were all leaving Vares and heading back to some village. I can't remember the name of the village. I set off on foot. Later the lorries left, went out of the town. Some people left in lorries; others would find cars. But on the whole, I know that an order had been issued according to which all cars, all vehicle, all appliances should be handed over in the barracks upon arrival in Zenica. I know someone who didn't hand some kind of a Zastava car over. A neighbour was with me. He took a car and sold it to someone for 400 German marks. He sold it for 400 German marks to someone. Later he had problems with the military police. They pursued him. I don't know exactly what happened. I think he may even have been imprisoned for that act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us earlier about seeing UNPROFOR troops in Vares. Did you have any contact with any UNPROFOR troops in Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They tried to provide some kind of protection. I don't know. The troops broke through -- broke into something, and they tried to prevent this. They said, "You're looting. Look at what you're doing. You're going to destroy the entire town." I can't remember everything, but I know that there was some sort of a quarrel with them, and an interpreter was present. He sounded like a Croat. And someone said, "What are you doing here, Ustasha?" And he turned around. I can't remember. I think there were two armoured vehicles there, and they then went to protect some other building. I don't know this for sure, but I heard that they went to protect UNHCR warehouses and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I think this might be an appropriate time for our next recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 25 to 6.00. We'll have a 25-minute break, and we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will resume our work now. It is eight minutes past 6.00. We can go on until 7.00. Mr. Mundis, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has completed its direct examination of the witness. We have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. We are now in open session. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness XE, you are now going to answer questions which will be put to you by Defence counsel, but I myself have a few small questions in order to clarify some questions put to you and which you have answered. You said that you were, as a nurse or as a medic, integrated within the 7th Muslim Brigade. When you were a member, did you receive a salary or were you a member without being paid? Did you receive a salary or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. I don't remember whether received some aid now and then in food, but not in money. As far as I can remember, we did receive any money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when you reported for recruitment, you were not obliged to join. You could have gone elsewhere. So you were recruited on a voluntary basis. It was your own decision to be recruited. And you didn't raise the question of a salary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were recruited, you became a soldier; right? And having become a soldier, were you given documents or military rules? Any documents of a religious nature? Were you given any documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us with a great deal of emotion in your voice a moment ago the bad treatment that you suffered. Being a high-level sportsman, you must have been accustomed to receiving blows. But the blows that you received were heavier than those that you received practicing your branch of sports on the sports arena?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was beaten by five or six men at the same time over there. They beat me with military boots and rods and wooden -- pieces of wood. No one is accustomed to being beaten like that. I don't know how you can imagine that anyone can be accustomed to being beaten with iron rods and wet towels. You don't find that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall now give the floor to the Defence for their questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before I begin with my cross-examination of this witness, the Defence teams for both accused would appeal to the Court for their understanding so that we could begin the cross-examination tomorrow, because according to the schedule the witness was planned for today and tomorrow morning. We have completed most of our preparations, but since the cross-examination is linked to the statement made by the witness here in the Tribunal - and he covered several areas - we feel that if we were to begin the cross-examination tomorrow the process would be simpler, easier for the witness, and thoroughly well prepared. There's also a small technical reason why we appeal to Your Honours for your indulgence: Namely, at the beginning of the proceedings today, we familiarised the Prosecutor with a previous statement by this witness given in the police station in Boden in Sweden, and we have not received the complete translation into B/C/S. This is a statement that I believe I will use in the cross-examination of this witness. And as the Prosecutor doesn't have it in translation, it should be translated overnight because the witness cannot follow the cross-examination if I show him the statement only in English. So for reasons of efficiency and in order for us to be better prepared, we appeal to Your Honours to allow us to begin our cross-examination tomorrow. But, of course, we will abide by the ruling of the Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, before taking a position on the request of the Defence, perhaps if my learned colleague or colleagues could give us some indication as to how long they anticipate their cross-examination lasting. We do have another witness scheduled for tomorrow. And as Your Honours are well aware, the Prosecution, being under certain time limits, as well as constraints on witnesses, before we take a stand on their request, if they could indicate a total amount of time for both Defence teams, if both teams will in fact be cross-examining, that could be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the rather complicated testimony, covering a wide range of topics, I believe that General Hadzihasanovic's Defence will need an hour and a half on the outside, if we organise ourselves properly and have all the translations ready and copied to be distributed to all the parties and Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence of Mr. Kubura will probably take about half an hour for the cross-examination. We would like to point out something else, that like the Defence for General Hadzihasanovic, we have been cooperative and sought to make the best of the time available to us. So I think this will not affect the possible testimony of the next witness who is planned for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no objection to commencing the cross-examination of the witness at the outset of tomorrow's courtroom schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber has heard both parties. If I understood correctly, the Defence will take one hour and a half for the cross-examination of this witness, and the Defence counsel for the second accused, about 30 minutes. So that will take a total of two hours, without any prejudice regarding possible re-examination by the Prosecution. Therefore, there is a chance for the second witness planned for tomorrow, that his testimony may not be completed tomorrow. We have 40 minutes left. Regardless of the technical reason that you have elaborated on, are there perhaps some questions that may be put to the witness without this affecting the questions planned for tomorrow? Would there not be some rather simple questions which could save some time tomorrow? This is just a suggestion that I am making. There may perhaps be some questions that don't require a great deal of reflection until tomorrow that could be put to the witness. Madam Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I certainly could ask some questions. But as I have said, I feel that if we were to have more time to put our thoughts in order, the cross-examination would be shorter. But perhaps I could start with some general questions for a period of 15 minutes. And after that, would you allow me to resume tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you will have about 15 minutes for some general questions, and then we will continue tomorrow. That will not be a problem. Therefore, Witness XE, you will have some general questions put to you by the Defence counsel, which will help us save some time for tomorrow, and we will continue tomorrow. You have the floor. We are now in open session. If you wish to go into private session, let me know, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. XE. My name is Edina Residovic. I am Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. I would like to ask you first of all to listen to the translation of my question in English and only then to provide an answer so that everyone in the courtroom can follow more easily. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. What am I supposed to wait for?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your headphones, you can hear the interpretation of my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So you want me to wait for it to be done into English?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't wait for the interpretation, then my question and your answer will overlap and those present in the courtroom who don't speak our language will not be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go into private session, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going into private session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The open session is continuing for me to be able to close the sitting. And as I have said, we will meet again tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 to continue the testimony of a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be recommenced on Tuesday, the 27th day of January, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.43 p.m.,
